one_line: AI products sold on claims that they do not and cannot live up to.
origin_note: Popularized by Princeton computer scientist Arvind Narayanan's 2019 talk 'How to recognize AI snake oil', later expanded into a newsletter and book.

sources.title: How to recognize AI snake oil (slides)

one_line: An AI assistant's tendency to flatter users, agree with them and validate their ideas whether or not they are right.
origin_note: An AI-safety term for a failure linked to training on human feedback; it drew mass attention in April 2025 when OpenAI rolled back an overly flattering GPT-4o update.

one_line: Overstating how much a product actually uses AI, or slapping 'AI-powered' on it, to impress customers and investors.
origin_note: Modeled on 'greenwashing'; Wikipedia says the AI Now Institute first defined it in 2019,.

one_line: Rewriting an existing text by swapping in synonyms and shuffled phrasing so it passes as new, usually to game search rankings or hide plagiarism.
origin_note: A black-hat SEO practice, done by hand or with automated 'spinner' software, that let sites dodge duplicate-content penalties; by 2024 the same trick was being run with generative AI.

one_line: Disguising an orchestrated campaign so it looks like spontaneous support from ordinary people.
origin_note: US senator Lloyd Bentsen is credited with the usage in 1985, contrasting real grass roots with AstroTurf brand artificial grass; online it now covers fake accounts, bots and coordinated posting.

one_line: Email you technically signed up for, such as alerts, newsletters and notifications, that piles up unread: better than spam, worse than real mail.
origin_note: Coined at a Pittsburgh conference (PodCamp Pittsburgh 2) in August 2007 as a pun on spam; NPR credited Canadian blogger Tommy Vallier with helping invent it.

sources.title: Move Over, Spam: 'Bacn' Is the E-Mail Dish du Jour

coined_by: Timothy R. Hannigan, Ian P. McCarthy and André Spicer
one_line: Made-up or inaccurate chatbot output that a person then uses uncritically in real work.
origin_note: Introduced by business scholars Hannigan, McCarthy and Spicer in 'Beware of botshit', published in Business Horizons in 2024; they frame it as what happens when humans pick up AI hallucinations and act on them.

sources.title: Beware of botshit: How to manage the epistemic risks of generative chatbots

one_line: The adage that refuting nonsense takes an order of magnitude more effort than producing it.
origin_note: Coined in 2013 by Italian programmer Alberto Brandolini; often cited when cheap, high-volume falsehood or slop swamps the people trying to correct it.

one_line: LinkedIn posts written one short sentence per line, building to a self-help or business lesson.
origin_note: The style spread on LinkedIn in late 2017, partly because line breaks force a 'see more' click that the algorithm reads as engagement; the coinage is variously credited to BuzzFeed News or Bloomberg writer Lorcan Roche Kelly.

sources.title: Broetry: Why is everyone suddenly writing in single line sentences on LinkedIn?
Meet the business leaders behind LinkedIn's 'broems' trend

one_line: Speech meant to persuade or impress without any regard for whether it is true.
origin_note: Philosopher Harry G. Frankfurt's 1986 essay On Bullshit became a 2005 bestselling book; his definition is now often applied to fluent but truth-indifferent chatbot output.

one_line: A grid of sensational thumbnail ads at the bottom of web pages that funnels readers to low-quality clickbait.
origin_note: Named after 'chumming', throwing fish scraps to attract fish; John Mahoney's 2015 article in The Awl popularized the term and catalogued its recurring themes.

one_line: News stories churned out by lightly rewriting press releases and wire copy instead of doing original reporting.
origin_note: A blend of 'churn' and 'journalism' credited to BBC journalist Waseem Zakir; Nick Davies popularized it in his 2008 book Flat Earth News.

one_line: A derogatory slang term for robots and AI systems, including chatbots.
origin_note: Used for battle droids in the 2005 game Star Wars: Republic Commando (and in earlier science fiction); in the 2020s, and especially 2025, it spread widely online as shorthand for distaste at AI being pushed into everyday life.

one_line: An operation where low-paid workers, or racks of phones, generate fake clicks, likes, follows and views to order.
origin_note: A form of click fraud that grew alongside social media metrics; it sells the look of popularity rather than any real audience.

one_line: A headline or thumbnail built to make you click, usually promising more than the content delivers.
origin_note: Merriam-Webster dates the word to 1999; it became the defining complaint about ad-funded web publishing in the 2010s as headlines were tuned for the 'curiosity gap'.

one_line: The idea that leaning on an AI assistant to do your thinking saves effort now but weakens your own engagement and memory later.
origin_note: Popularized by the 2025 MIT Media Lab study 'Your Brain on ChatGPT', which compared brain activity of people writing essays with and without an LLM.

sources.title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task

one_line: A company that pumps out huge volumes of cheap articles or videos aimed at search and ad revenue rather than readers.
origin_note: Associated with sites like Demand Media's eHow around 2009–2010, which Google targeted with its 2011 Panda update; since 2023 NewsGuard has tracked thousands of AI-run content farms.

sources.title: Tracking AI-enabled Misinformation: AI Content Farm sites

one_line: The point where the amount of content being produced outstrips people's limited capacity to consume it.
origin_note: Marketing writer Mark Schaefer coined it in a January 6, 2014 blog post arguing content marketing was not a sustainable strategy for most businesses.

sources.title: The Blog Post That Shocked the World

one_line: A block of text copied and pasted across the internet over and over, often as a joke or to bait reactions.
origin_note: From 'copy and paste'; Merriam-Webster and Wikipedia trace it to 4chan and Usenet in 2006.

one_line: The word 'delve' and similar favourites ('underscore', 'meticulous', 'showcasing') used as a giveaway that text was written or polished by an LLM.
origin_note: Studies of millions of PubMed abstracts found 'delves' and other style words jumped abruptly after ChatGPT's release, estimating at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were LLM-processed.

sources.title: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary
sources.publisher: arXiv (Kobak et al.; published in Science Advances)

one_line: Compulsively scrolling through bad news or upsetting content even though it makes you feel worse.
origin_note: First documented in a 2018 tweet and spread widely during the COVID-19 pandemic; Macquarie Dictionary named it a 2020 word of the year.

one_line: A page made only to rank for a particular search query, which then funnels visitors somewhere else.
origin_note: An old black-hat SEO technique; Google's spam policies now call it 'doorway abuse', such as near-identical pages targeting every city name.

sources.title: Spam policies for Google web search

one_line: The scandal over mass-produced, keyword-stuffed YouTube videos that looked child-friendly but showed disturbing or inappropriate content.
origin_note: Named after Elsa from Frozen, the term was coined online in 2017; channels existed from 2014, and James Bridle's November 2017 essay drew wide attention to algorithm-driven kids' video.

one_line: A propaganda method of pumping out a fast, constant, high-volume stream of messages with no commitment to truth or consistency.
origin_note: RAND researchers used the phrase in 2016 to characterize contemporary Russian propaganda: many channels, many messages, and a shameless willingness to spread partial truths or fictions.

sources.title: The Russian "Firehose of Falsehood" Propaganda Model

one_line: A strategy of overwhelming the public with so much content and claims that no one can keep up or sort truth from noise.
origin_note: Steve Bannon described it to Michael Lewis in 2018 ("flood the zone with shit"); it is now a common description of volume-over-accuracy messaging.

one_line: When an AI model states false or made-up information as if it were fact.
origin_note: Borrowed loosely from psychology; Cambridge Dictionary added the AI sense in 2023. Some researchers prefer 'confabulation' or 'bullshitting' to avoid anthropomorphizing.

one_line: A quickly produced, deliberately provocative opinion on the news, high on heat and low on research.
origin_note: From sports talk radio; Merriam-Webster dates it to 2012, and John Herrman's 2014 piece in The Awl tied it to the economics of online publishing.

one_line: A boast disguised as modesty or complaint, as in 'so tired from accepting all these awards'.
origin_note: Comedian Harris Wittels used it as the name of his @Humblebrag Twitter account in 2010 and wrote a 2012 book on it; the American Dialect Society named it 2011's most useful word.

one_line: Social media content that glorifies working punishing hours and grinding without rest as the path to success.
origin_note: Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian criticized it in talks such as a 2019 Wall Street Journal festival appearance, calling it one of the most toxic things in tech.

sources.title: Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian blasts 'hustle porn' on social media: It's 'really toxic'

one_line: An overabundance of information, accurate and not, that spreads alongside a crisis and makes reliable guidance hard to find.
origin_note: Coined by David Rothkopf in a May 2003 Washington Post column about SARS; it became widely used in 2020 when the WHO applied it to COVID-19.

one_line: Having so much information coming at you that it becomes harder, not easier, to understand things and make decisions.
origin_note: Used by management scholars in the 1960s (Bertram Gross, 1964) and popularized by Alvin Toffler's 1970 Future Shock; 'infobesity' is a later web-era variant.

one_line: Contamination of the information supply with irrelevant, redundant, unsolicited or low-value material.
origin_note: Framed as the digital equivalent of industrial pollution; the term gained traction in 2003 through usability expert Jakob Nielsen's writing.

one_line: A 2025 meme wave of absurd AI-generated creatures with mock-Italian names and synthetic voiceovers, such as Tralalero Tralala.
origin_note: Emerged on TikTok in January 2025 and spread to Instagram and beyond; Wikipedia notes its sloppy aesthetics and nonsense narratives as part of the appeal.

one_line: Cramming a page with repeated search terms, lists of place names or hidden text so it ranks, at the cost of readability.
origin_note: One of the oldest forms of spamdexing, a word recorded as early as 1996; Google's spam policies still list it by name.

sources.title: Spam policies for Google web search

one_line: A label, from a popular Reddit community, for cringe-inducing, self-aggrandizing or absurd posts on LinkedIn.
origin_note: The subreddit r/LinkedInLunatics was launched on October 1, 2019 and had over 540,000 followers by June 2024 by collecting the platform's strangest posts.

one_line: An article built as a numbered list, often padded around a thin idea for quick clicks.
origin_note: A blend of 'list' and 'article' that Merriam-Webster dates to 2007; it became a staple of viral publishers and a by-word for cheap content creation.

one_line: Flooding the web with propaganda so it gets swept into AI training data and search results and repeated by chatbots.
origin_note: Named in a 2025 American Sunlight Project report on the pro-Russia 'Pravda' network; NewsGuard later found leading chatbots repeating its narratives about a third of the time.

sources.title: Russian networks flood the Internet with propaganda, aiming to corrupt AI chatbots
A Well-funded Moscow-based Global 'News' Network has Infected Western Artificial Intelligence Tools Worldwide with Russian Propaganda

one_line: A website with no real value of its own, built only to draw visitors in and get them to click on ads.
origin_note: A derogatory SEO-era label for scraper and filler sites built around Google AdSense; considered search spam that dilutes results.

one_line: The degradation of AI models trained on output from other AI models, which lose the rare and varied parts of real data over generations.
origin_note: Named by Shumailov and colleagues in a 2023 preprint and their 2024 Nature paper; the nickname 'Habsburg AI' compares it to royal inbreeding.

sources.title: AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data
The Curse of Recursion: Training on Generated Data Makes Models Forget

one_line: Media designed to make you angry, served up because indignation drives views, shares and comments.
origin_note: Coined by cartoonist and essayist Tim Kreider in a July 2009 New York Times piece.

one_line: Low-cost, often templated or automated 'local news' sites that look independent but quietly serve a political or commercial agenda.
origin_note: Coined by journalist Ryan Smith in 2012 after the meat-filler nickname; the Columbia Journalism Review counted more than 1,200 such sites by 2020.

one_line: Online content deliberately designed to make people angry so they engage with it.
origin_note: First recorded on Usenet in 2002; Oxford University Press named it the 2025 Word of the Year.

sources.title: The Oxford Word of the Year 2025 is rage bait

one_line: Someone, usually a man, who compulsively replies to other people's posts, especially women's or famous accounts', in an unwanted or condescending way.
origin_note: Used neutrally from around 2012 (an Applebee's social media manager was dubbed its 'Reply Guy'); by 2015 it had become a pejorative.

one_line: Google's term for generating many pages, by AI, scraping or cheap writers, mainly to manipulate search rankings rather than help readers.
origin_note: Introduced as a named spam policy in Google's March 2024 core update, alongside expired domain abuse and site reputation abuse.

sources.title: What web creators should know about our March 2024 core update and new spam policies
Spam policies for Google web search

one_line: A website that copies other sites' content wholesale and republishes it to earn ad money.
origin_note: Scraper sites mirror other pages to earn ad revenue; Google's 2024 policies also cover AI-'transformed' scraped content.

sources.title: Spam policies for Google web search

one_line: Posting deliberately absurd, low-quality or provocative content, often ironically, to derail a conversation or get a rise.
origin_note: Merriam-Webster finds the word in the 1990s; it took its current ironic form on image boards like 4chan in the mid-2000s and became a political tactic around 2016.

one_line: Publishing low-value third-party pages on a trusted website to borrow its search ranking, such as casino reviews on a news or university site.
origin_note: Google named it as a spam policy in March 2024; SEO practitioners commonly call the tactic parasite SEO.

sources.title: What web creators should know about our March 2024 core update and new spam policies
Spam policies for Google web search

one_line: A mocking label for someone who relies on AI chatbots for everything, from what to order to how to reply to a text.
origin_note: Spread on TikTok in mid-2025 and was picked up by Rusty Foster's Today in Tabs and Futurism.

sources.title: People Are Becoming "Sloppers" Who Have to Ask AI Before They Do Anything

one_line: Registering software package names that AI coding tools hallucinate, so that developers who trust the suggestion install malware.
origin_note: Coined in April 2025 by Python Software Foundation security developer Seth Larson and popularized by Andrew Nesbitt; a play on typosquatting.

one_line: Split-screen short videos that stack unrelated clips, like Family Guy over Subway Surfers gameplay, to hold attention.
origin_note: Grew out of tricks to evade copyright detection on YouTube compilations and became a TikTok and Shorts staple; raised concerns about very young viewers.

one_line: A fake online identity used to praise yourself, attack critics or fake a crowd.
origin_note: Long-standing internet slang; also used in stealth marketing and as a building block of troll farms and astroturfing.

one_line: A fake blog filled with scraped or junk text, made only to boost other sites' search rankings or serve ads.
origin_note: The word 'splog' was popularized around August 2005 when Mark Cuban used it publicly.

coined_by: Emily M. Bender, Timnit Gebru and co-authors
one_line: A description of large language models as systems that stitch together plausible language without understanding what it means.
origin_note: From the 2021 paper 'On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big?' presented at ACM FAccT; the American Dialect Society nominated it as 2023's AI-related word of the year.

sources.title: Stochastic Parrots (paper and media coverage)
sources.publisher: Emily M. Bender, University of Washington

one_line: An organized group paid to post propaganda and harassment using fake or coordinated accounts.
origin_note: Best known from Russia's Internet Research Agency and its interference around the 2016 US election; Freedom House found 30 governments paying such 'keyboard armies' in 2017.

one_line: Posting something cryptic and context-free, like 'some people, honestly', to fish for concern or questions.
origin_note: 'Vaguebooking' was coined for deliberately vague Facebook statuses; 'vagueposting' is the platform-neutral form.

one_line: A string of words and phrases that sound like language but add up to no clear meaning.
origin_note: Originally a psychiatric term for disorganized speech; in everyday use it is a put-down for empty, incoherent answers, and is now often applied to rambling AI text.
